title: Smallest degree of a Keller counterexample in dimension 3
W: In 2026 the Jacobian conjecture was refuted in three variables. The first explicit counterexample (Alpöge's map) has polynomial degree 7. Wang's theorem says degree 2 is impossible. What is the smallest degree a counterexample in three variables can have? In particular, is there one of degree 3, 4 or 5?
M: Let $d_3$ be the least $d$ such that some polynomial map $F:\mathbb C^3\to\mathbb C^3$ with $\max_i\deg F_i=d$ and $\det DF\in\mathbb C^\times$ is not an automorphism. Wang's theorem gives $d_3\ge3$, and Alpöge's map gives $d_3\le7$. Determine $d_3$. In particular, decide whether $d_3\le5$.
why: Once the conjecture is false in dimension 3, the main remaining question is how much room counterexamples need. Wang's quadratic theorem and the Bass–Connell–Wright cubic-homogeneous reduction both point to low degree as the decisive regime. Settling $d_3$ means either proving the conjecture for all cubic, quartic or quintic maps in three variables, which would be new even for cubics, or finding a much smaller counterexample. The answer tells us whether the phenomenon is rigid or flexible.
issues: The original 'degree 5 or less' was arbitrary, so I recast it as determining the minimal degree $d_3\in[3,7]$ and kept the $\le5$ question as the special case. Known facts: Alpöge's map (degrees 7,6,4; Jacobian -2; generically 3-to-1), a second map G (degrees 4,11,12), and Gallagher's family of every geometric degree $\ge3$ (polynomial degrees not stated in the sources I read). Wang excludes degree 2. 'Degree' must mean polynomial degree, not geometric/fibre degree, because the 2026 papers use both. The general (nonhomogeneous) cubic case in dimension 3 does not appear to be settled in the literature I found. Section 8 of arXiv:2607.20210 shows that for fixed bounded degrees, existence over an algebraically closed field is decidable by elimination. So small cases may be attackable by computation, which is a risk that this gets settled quickly. Wright's cubic-homogeneous result in dimension 3 is recalled from memory and was not re-checked. I found no source that poses the minimal-degree question explicitly.

title: Forced blow-up up to the Lions threshold
W: With an ordinary Laplacian, a smooth compactly supported push can make a fluid at rest blow up in finite time (OpenAI, 2026). With dissipation (-Δ)^α for α ≥ 5/4, Lions proved that solutions stay smooth. Does forced blow-up from rest still happen for every α strictly between 1 and 5/4?
M:
For $\alpha\in(1,5/4)$ consider $\partial_tu+(u\cdot
abla)u+
abla p=-(-\Delta)^{\alpha}u+f$, $
abla\cdot u=0$ on $\mathbb R^3$, $u(\cdot,0)=0$. Decide whether for every such $\alpha$ there is $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3	imes(0,\infty);\mathbb R^3)$ for which the smooth solution breaks down in finite time, i.e. $\limsup_{t\uparrow T}\|u(t)\|_{L^\infty}=\infty$ for some $T<\infty$.
why: Lions' threshold $\alpha=5/4$ is exactly where energy-level dissipation becomes critical, so it is the natural candidate for the sharp boundary between regularity and singularity. The 2026 construction of forced blow-up at $\alpha=1$ makes the forced form of this question meaningful. Pushing it to every $\alpha<5/4$ would show that the energy-critical exponent is the true dividing line, at least when forcing is allowed.
issues: As written the range '$\alpha<5/4$' included $\alpha=1$, which is a form of Clay's forced statement and was claimed in 2026 by OpenAI. That paper proves smooth, compactly supported, time-dependent force, zero data, all $\nu>0$, not yet refereed. Cao–Chi–Nie use it as a black box. I restricted to $\alpha\in(1,5/4)$ and changed 'construct' to 'decide'. Hypodissipative forced blow-up is known for $\alpha<\alpha_0\approx0.093$ with a rougher force (arXiv:2407.06776). None of the sources treat $\alpha>1$ or mention Lions' threshold. Breakdown is defined via $L^\infty$.

title: Blow-up under a steady force
W: The 2026 forced Navier–Stokes blow-up uses a push that varies in time and is switched on and off. Can a smooth, compactly supported push that never changes in time also drive a fluid at rest to a singularity?
M:
Decide whether there is $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$, independent of $t$, such that the solution of $\partial_tu+(u\cdot
abla)u+
abla p=\Delta u+f$, $
abla\cdot u=0$, $u(\cdot,0)=0$ on $\mathbb R^3$ loses smoothness in finite time.
why: Steady stirring is the physically basic forcing, and a time-independent force cannot be tuned to the scales of a developing singularity. A positive answer would mean the singularity is produced by the nonlinearity alone under a fixed energy input. A negative answer would show that the time-dependent forcing in known constructions is essential.
issues: Before 2026 this was a strengthening of Clay's forced statement. After OpenAI's claimed time-dependent forced blow-up (force supported away from $t=0$, not yet refereed) it is the natural next step. Only gradient forces are excluded trivially, since they give the zero solution (Cao–Chi–Nie Prop. 3.17), so $f$ must have a nontrivial solenoidal part. Heuristic: a bounded steady force is subcritical at small scales, so near the singular point the blow-up is essentially unforced. This is probably far harder than the time-dependent case and close to Millennium level, which limits its value as a list item. I changed the wording to 'decide'.

title: Prime-sum labelling of balanced trees
W: (As stated, false.) Label a tree with 1 to n so every edge sum is prime. The fixable version: does balance plus bounded maximum degree suffice for large n?
M: (Corrected, grade C.) Fix $\Delta\ge3$. Is there $n_0(\Delta)$ such that every tree on $n\ge n_0$ vertices with maximum degree $\le\Delta$ and bipartition classes of sizes $\lceil n/2\rceil,\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ admits a bijection $V\to[n]$ with every edge sum prime?
why: It extends the classical prime-circle and prime-path arrangements of $1,\dots,n$ (Greenfield–Greenwood) from paths to trees. It mixes the distribution of primes in short intervals with tree embedding.
issues: FALSE as stated. Take a vertex v adjacent to all of the other class (a caterpillar: v joined to all $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ vertices of class B, the remaining A-vertices hung off one B-vertex). This tree is balanced, but v's label a would need a+b prime for every b of the opposite parity in [n], which is impossible once n is moderately large. More generally deg(v) is at most the number of primes in (a,a+n], about n/log n. Brute force over all balanced trees: failures at n=7..14 number 2,3,7,6,12,9,53,64 (n=14: 64 of 895). Every failing tree had max degree $\ge4$, and all balanced trees with $\Delta\le3$ up to n=14 were labellable. The bounded-degree repair is plausible but narrow, grade C at best.

title: Information-tight sorting of pattern classes
W: An array is promised to avoid a fixed pattern. Counting the allowed orders gives a lower bound on the comparisons needed to sort it, and Fredman's theorem says this bound plus 2n always suffices. Opler (2024) showed the right order of magnitude is linear. Is the counting bound tight up to lower-order terms, o(n), for every pattern?
M: For a permutation $\tau$ let $C_\tau(n)$ be the minimum worst-case number of comparisons of a decision tree that sorts $a_1,\dots,a_n$ under the promise that their order pattern lies in $\mathrm{Av}_n(\tau)$. Fredman: $\log_2|\mathrm{Av}_n(\tau)|\le C_\tau(n)\le\log_2|\mathrm{Av}_n(\tau)|+2n$. Decide whether $C_\tau(n)=\log_2|\mathrm{Av}_n(\tau)|+o(n)$ for every $\tau$, and in particular for $\tau=1324$.
why: The comparison model is one of the few settings where information-theoretic lower bounds are often nearly exact. Even for unrestricted sorting it is unknown whether $\log_2 n!+o(n)$ comparisons suffice. Pattern classes give a family where this question is harder to dismiss. A linear gap for some $\tau$ would need a new lower-bound technique, and tightness for every $\tau$ would need a strong structural sorting algorithm.
issues: Opler (arXiv:2409.07868) gives $O((\log c_\tau+1)n)$, tight up to a constant factor, but not the additive $o(n)$ question. I found nowhere that poses the additive form. Small cases: for $\tau\in\{132,231,312,213\}$ (equivalent under reversal and complement, which preserve the sorting problem; inverse does not), stack sorting uses $\le2n$ comparisons and $\log_2 C_n=2n-O(\log n)$, so the answer is yes. $\tau\in\{123,321\}$ seems tractable by an adaptive merge but I did not check it. The question is substantive only for $|\tau|\ge4$. I stated that the decision tree knows $\tau$.

title: Outer billiards around a superellipse
W: Outer billiards around a smooth convex shape with positive curvature has only bounded orbits (Moser–Douady). Polygons and generic C¹ shapes can have unbounded orbits. Decide what happens for the analytic shape x⁴+y⁴ ≤ 1, whose curvature vanishes at four points.
M: Let $K=\{x^4+y^4\le1\}$ and let $T:\mathbb R^2\setminus K\to\mathbb R^2\setminus K$ be the outer billiard map: $T(p)=2q-p$, where $q\in\partial K$ is the point of tangency of the right-hand tangent line from $p$. Decide whether every $T$-orbit is bounded.
why: Douady's proof needs $C^6$ and positive curvature. At a flat point the inverse Gauss map is only Hölder (the support function here is $C^{1,1/3}$), so the twist map at infinity is not smooth enough for KAM. Unbounded orbits are known for some polygons (Schwartz), semicircles (Dolgopyat–Fayad) and generic $C^1$ symmetric tables. This analytic example tests whether isolated flat points alone can destroy confinement.
issues: I found no treatment of tables with isolated zero-curvature points. The 2026 $C^1$-generic result (arXiv:2610.06418) covers tables whose radius-of-curvature measure is purely singular, which is not this case: here it is absolutely continuous with integrable singularities $\sim|\theta|^{-2/3}$. T is well defined because $K$ is strictly convex. Numerical check: one orbit starting at $\ell^4$-gauge 30.7, run for $1.18\times10^6$ steps, stayed in gauge [21.55, 30.82] with no drift, which is weak evidence for boundedness. The statement is unchanged.

title: Rotation-proof lattice-point-poor shapes
W: Among convex shapes of area A, how few lattice points can a shape be guaranteed to contain under every rotation about the origin? Can any shape do much better than a disc centred at the origin?
M: For $A>0$ let $m(A)=\inf\{\sup_{\theta}\#(\rho_\theta K\cap\mathbb Z^2): K\subset\mathbb R^2\text{ compact convex},\ |K|=A\}$. Decide whether $m(A)\ge A-O_\varepsilon(A^{1/4+\varepsilon})$.
why: It is a rotation-uniform form of the Gauss circle problem. An origin-centred disc is rotation-invariant, and its deficit $A-N(\sqrt{A/\pi})$ can reach order $A^{1/4}$ (Hardy–Landau). The question is whether any convex body does essentially better.
issues: The original 'determine the convex K … to second-order term' is ill-posed. The optimiser depends on A arithmetically. For discs the value is the circle-problem count $N(R)$, which oscillates, so there is no definite second-order term. I replaced it with a definite inequality question. Heuristic: sup over rotations is at least the rotation average $\sum_n r_2(n)\,\theta_K(\sqrt n)/2\pi$, which differs from A by a small smoothed error, so a deficit much larger than $A^{1/4}$ seems unlikely. The problem stays tied to circle-problem exponents and is fairly arbitrary. My searches found no direct literature.

title: Deciding rationality of PL rotation numbers
W: A circle homeomorphism made of finitely many straight pieces, with rational break points and slopes, has a rotation number. Rational rotation numbers can be confirmed by finding a rational periodic orbit. Irrational ones occur too: Belk–Hyde–Moore found √2−1 with slopes 3/2, 2/3, 1. Is there an algorithm that always decides which case holds?
M: Let $\mathcal P$ be the set of orientation-preserving PL homeomorphisms of $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with finitely many rational break points, rational slopes and $f(0)\in\mathbb Q$, encoded by these data. Is $\{f\in\mathcal P:\rho(f)\in\mathbb Q\}$ decidable? (It is computably enumerable: if $\rho(f)=p/q$, the zero set of the lift $F^q(x)-x-p$ is a nonempty finite union of rational points and rational intervals.)
why: Rotation numbers of rational PL maps link Thompson-like groups $T_q$, renormalisation, and number theory. Belk–Hyde–Moore conjecture that the irrational values are quadratic when slopes are powers of one rational, and they ask about decidability for one-parameter families and for finite order in $T_q$. A decision procedure would amount to a structure theorem for when renormalisation of such maps fails to close up.
issues: Belk–Hyde–Moore (arXiv:2211.05825) give an explicit rational map with $\rho=\sqrt2-1$, refuting Calegari's question. Their Questions 3–4 are close relatives (deciding for the family $f_{q,r}$, and finite order in $T_q$) but not this exact question, and I found no paper posing it. The c.e. direction checks out. $\rho$ is computable, which only helps for a fixed candidate $p/q$. The statement is clean; I added the encoding and the c.e. justification.

title: L⁴ Strichartz on the surface of a cube
W: On a square torus, the L⁴ Strichartz estimate for the Schrödinger equation loses only ε derivatives (Bourgain). On general flat surfaces with cone points only a 1/4-derivative loss is known. Decide whether the cube surface, with eight cone points of angle 3π/2 that diffract waves, behaves like the torus.
M: Let $S$ be the surface of the unit cube with its flat metric, and $\Delta$ the Friedrichs extension of the Laplacian from $C_c^\infty(S\setminus\{\text{vertices}\})$. Decide whether for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $C_\varepsilon$ with $\|e^{it\Delta}f\|_{L^4([0,1]\times S)}\le C_\varepsilon\|f\|_{H^\varepsilon(S)}$ for all $f$.
why: The cube surface is an arithmetic surface with cone points. Its 'nonsingular' eigenfunctions lift to trigonometric polynomials (Greif–Kaplan–Strichartz–Wiese), but the singular ones are not explicit, and diffraction at the vertices spoils the lattice-counting proof used on the torus. Blair–Ford–Marzuola obtain a $1/p$ loss on all compact flat cone surfaces and suggest the loss is an artefact of their method. The cube is the simplest test case where arithmetic structure and diffraction compete.
issues: Sources: Blair–Ford–Marzuola Thm 1.5 gives a $H^{1/4}$ bound for p=q=4 on compact Euclidean surfaces with conical singularities, and Remark 1.3 suggests the loss is not sharp. I found no ε-loss result for any surface whose cone angles are not of the form $2\pi/k$; pillowcase-type quotients of tori are easy. I specified the Friedrichs extension and changed 'prove' to 'decide', since the truth is unclear. The estimate would force $\|\varphi\|_{L^4}\lesssim\lambda^{\varepsilon}$ for the singular eigenfunctions and needs near-coincidence counting for an irregular spectrum.

title: Ising spin at a cube corner
W: Glue three quarter-planes of the square grid into the surface of an infinite cube corner (a flat cone of angle 3π/2) and run the critical Ising model. Prove that the spin at the corner decorrelates with the exponent 7/24 predicted by conformal field theory.
M: Let $\Gamma$ be the union of the three quadrant lattices $\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^2$ on the faces of $\partial\mathbb R_{\ge0}^3$, glued along the coordinate axes, with apex $o$ (degree 3; every other vertex has degree 4). Let $\langle\cdot\rangle$ be the infinite-volume limit of the nearest-neighbour Ising model at $\beta_c=\tfrac12\log(1+\sqrt2)$ with free boundary conditions on $\Gamma\cap\{\|x\|_\infty\le n\}$. Prove $\langle\sigma_o\sigma_x\rangle\asymp|x|^{-7/24}$ as $|x|\to\infty$.
why: Rigorous conformal invariance of Ising spin correlations (Chelkak–Hongler–Izyurov) is proved for planar domains, and a conical point is the simplest source of curvature. Under $w=z^{4/3}$ the apex spin acquires scaling dimension $\tfrac{2\pi}{\alpha}\cdot\tfrac18=\tfrac16$, so the two-point exponent is $\tfrac16+\tfrac18=\tfrac7{24}$. This exponent depends on the geometry and differs from both the bulk value $1/4$ and the corner values. Proving it would extend discrete complex analysis to cone singularities.
issues: I checked the CFT computation: $|w|^{-1/4}|w'(x)|^{1/8}$ with $w=z^{4/3}$ gives $|x|^{-1/3+1/24}=|x|^{-7/24}$. Physics papers confirm CFT predictions numerically for conical lattices (Costa-Santos, free-energy log terms), but I found no rigorous spin-exponent result on cones. Chelkak–Izyurov–Mahfouf (arXiv:2104.12858) and CHI cover only planar or isoradial planar settings. I specified β_c and the infinite-volume measure, which were missing, and noted that the gluing is a locally flat square lattice away from $o$. Risk: this may be within reach of existing spinor and s-holomorphic methods.
